full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. CARLOS RACADIO ASUNCION, MAMELFA R. AMONGOL, GENOVEVA R. RAGASA, ROSITA R. RAGUNJAN, AND VIRGINIA R. RAFANAN, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: IV. Special Penal Laws > E. Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019, as amended by BP 195 and RA 10910)
topics: Sec. 3(e), RA 3019: evident bad faith, manifest partiality, gross inexcusable negligence
Erroneous interpretation of a law in good faith is not bad faith
Sec. 3(j), RA 3019: knowledge of the grantee's lack of qualification is essential
RA 3019 violations must be grounded on graft and corruption (Martel v. People)
Malversation and conspiracy not proved; no presumption of bad faith

doctrine:
To convict under **Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019**, the prosecution must prove that the public officer acted through manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence. **An erroneous interpretation of a provision of law, absent any dishonest or wrongful purpose, is not bad faith** (reiterating *Ysidoro v. Leonardo-De Castro*); bad faith must be *evident*, partaking of fraud and showing a manifest deliberate intent to do wrong or cause damage. Manifest partiality requires a clear, notorious or plain inclination to favor one side over another, and gross inexcusable negligence is negated where the officer relied on Sanggunian accreditations, resolutions and appropriation ordinances. Repayment of the amounts upon COA disallowance is a badge of good faith.

**Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019 requires proof that the officer *knowingly* granted a privilege or benefit to one not qualified or not legally entitled to it.** Knowledge of the grantee's lack of qualification is essential because it is the basis for concluding that the officer acted with bias or partiality, and possibly corruption. **Violations of RA 3019 must be grounded on graft and corruption**: it is not enough that an official violated a law or rule, resulting in gain to a private person and damage to the government, if the root of the gain and damage is mere mistake (reiterating *Martel v. People*).

Malversation under Art. 217 of the RPC fails where the disbursement was supported by an appropriation ordinance, including one deemed reenacted under **Sec. 323 of the Local Government Code**. **Conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt** by overt acts showing a conscious common design; the mayor's marriage to the president of the beneficiary federation is not enough. **There is no presumption of bad faith in cases involving violations of RA 3019.**
facts:
Carlos R. Asuncion was mayor of Sta. Catalina, Ilocos Sur for three consecutive terms from 2007 to 2016. His wife Flora was the Federated President of the Bayanihan ng Kababaihan, an organization of women rural workers. Co-accused Amongol, Ragunjan, Rafanan and Ragasa were the presidents of its Cabittaogan, Subec, Paratong and Sinabaan chapters. The organization was accredited by the Sangguniang Bayan on September 20, 2010; the defense showed Sanggunian resolutions accrediting it as a community-based NGO and civil society organization since 2007.

On June 4, 2012, Asuncion approved four undated project proposals and signed four memoranda of agreement with the chapter presidents. Each chapter received PHP 100,000.00, released by checks dated June 15, 2012, as financial assistance for livelihood projects; the recipient members were to repay within six months with interest. The funds came from the municipality's 2010 share in the tobacco excise tax under RA 7171. The COA disallowed the disbursements, and the chapters returned the full amounts on February 22, 2016, before the criminal cases were filed.

On complaint of Jonathan Redoble, an opposition member and son of Asuncion's three-time rival, the Ombudsman charged all five with four counts each of violation of Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019, violation of Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019, and malversation of public funds. The prosecution claimed that the chapters lacked legal personality (not registered with the SEC, the CDA or DOLE), were not associations of tobacco farmers, and received the funds without Sanggunian authority or appropriation. The parties submitted a joint stipulation of facts in lieu of witnesses. The defense invoked the accreditations, Sangguniang Bayan Resolution No. 39, s. 2010 authorizing the mayor to sign contracts for the municipality, Appropriation Ordinance No. 01, s. 2010, reenacted in 2011 and 2012 under Sec. 323 of the LGC, and good faith.

The Sandiganbayan (Fourth Division) convicted all five on all counts, finding conspiracy, and denied reconsideration. They appealed. Rafanan filed her appellant's brief belatedly; the Court admitted it in the interest of substantial justice, noting that she and her counsel live in Ilocos Sur and the difficulty of filing during the pandemic lockdowns.
issues: Whether the Sandiganbayan erred in finding a conspiracy between Mayor Asuncion and the chapter presidents of the Bayanihan ng Kababaihan.
Whether the Sandiganbayan erred in holding that the guilt of the accused for violation of Sections 3(e) and 3(j) of RA 3019 and for malversation of public funds was proved beyond reasonable doubt.
ruling:
**1. Yes, conspiracy was not proved.** The prosecution's only evidence of conspiracy was the Asuncions' marriage certificate and Flora's certification that she was the Federated President. Inferring a conspiracy in bad faith from the marriage alone "requires a big leap of the imagination." There is no presumption of bad faith in RA 3019 cases; conviction must rest on the strength of the prosecution's evidence. Conspiracy must be shown with the same degree of proof required for the crime, through overt acts showing a conscious common design (*Macairan v. People*; *Suba v. Sandiganbayan*). No nexus showed a unity of action and purpose to give unwarranted benefits to the chapter presidents. With no conspiracy, the mayor's acquittal carried with it the acquittal of the chapter presidents, absent other evidence of their guilt.

**2. Yes, guilt was not proved beyond reasonable doubt on any charge.**

*Sec. 3(e).* The first two elements (public officer acting in his official functions) were undisputed, but the third was absent. Sec. 2 of RA 7171 lists projects for the self-reliance of tobacco farmers but does not specifically exclude other farmers in the province, and Sec. 14 of RA 11346 later enlarged the use of the fund. The many circulars on the fund's use show how easily local executives err. Without an express exclusion, Asuncion could be excused for believing, albeit mistakenly, that the chapters could borrow from the fund, especially as tobacco farmers lived in their barangays. Under *Ysidoro v. Leonardo-De Castro*, an erroneous interpretation of law, absent a dishonest or wrongful purpose, is not bad faith, and bad faith must be evident. There was no manifest partiality, since the prosecution did not claim that other borrowers were unjustly set aside. There was no gross inexcusable negligence, since he relied on the Sanggunian accreditations, Resolution No. 39, s. 2010, and the reenacted Appropriation Ordinance No. 01, s. 2010. The repayment upon disallowance and before the filing of the cases is a badge of good faith.

*Sec. 3(j).* The element of knowledge was not proved. Given the Sanggunian's (and later DOLE's) accreditation, any lack of qualification of the chapters "would not have been apparent to anyone," including the mayor.

*Graft and corruption.* Under *Martel v. People*, a charge under RA 3019 must be grounded on graft and corruption. The loans rested on a mistaken belief in good faith; there was no evidence of a bribe or of personal gain by any accused. The Court should not interpret the law so as to punish "every minute mistake that incidentally caused a benefit to private parties."

*Malversation.* The decisive element, that the accused appropriated, took or misappropriated public funds or consented to or, through abandonment or negligence, permitted their taking, was not proved. No contract involving public funds may be entered into without a sufficient appropriation (PD 1445, Sec. 85), but here the disbursements were supported by Appropriation Ordinance No. 01, s. 2010, reenacted in 2011 and 2012 under Sec. 323 of the LGC.
disposition: The appeal was GRANTED. The Sandiganbayan (Fourth Division) Decision dated May 17, 2019 in Case Nos. SB-17-CRM-1393 to 1404 and its Resolution dated August 14, 2019 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Carlos R. Asuncion, Mamelfa R. Amongol, Genoveva R. Ragasa, Rosita Ragunjan and Virginia R. Rafanan were ACQUITTED for failure of the prosecution to prove their guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Entry of judgment was ordered issued immediately.

bar_questions.q: Mayor Ana released PHP 500,000.00 from the municipality's share in the tobacco excise tax under RA 7171 as livelihood loans to a farmers' association accredited by the Sangguniang Bayan, whose members grow rice and vegetables in the tobacco-producing province. She relied on a Sangguniang Bayan resolution authorizing her to sign contracts for the municipality and on the reenacted annual appropriation ordinance. The COA disallowed the release on the ground that only tobacco farmers may benefit, and the association repaid the loans in full before any case was filed. There is no evidence that Mayor Ana received anything from the association or turned away other applicants. She is charged with violation of Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019. Is she liable?

alac.answer: No. Mayor Ana is not liable under Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019.
alac.legal_basis: Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019 requires, among others, that the public officer acted through manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence. An erroneous interpretation of a provision of law, absent any dishonest or wrongful purpose, is not bad faith; bad faith must be evident and partake of fraud. Reliance on Sanggunian accreditations, resolutions and appropriation ordinances negates gross inexcusable negligence, and repayment upon COA disallowance is a badge of good faith. Violations of RA 3019 must be grounded on graft and corruption, not mere mistake (People v. Asuncion, G.R. Nos. 250366 and 250388-98, April 6, 2022, citing Ysidoro v. Leonardo-De Castro and Martel v. People).
alac.application: RA 7171 does not expressly exclude other farmers in a tobacco-producing province, so Mayor Ana's belief that the association qualified, even if mistaken, was an honest interpretation of the law. She relied on the Sangguniang Bayan's accreditation, its resolution authorizing her to contract, and the reenacted appropriation ordinance, so she did not act without even slight care. Nothing shows that she favored the association over other applicants, and the full repayment before any case was filed, with no evidence of personal gain, shows the absence of corrupt intent.
alac.conclusion: Mayor Ana should be acquitted because the mode of commission required by Sec. 3(e) is absent.

bar_questions.q: Suppose instead that a municipal ordinance allowed livelihood loans from the fund only to organizations accredited by the Sangguniang Bayan, that the association had never been accredited, and that before approving the loans Mayor Ana received a written memorandum from the municipal accountant pointing this out. She approved the loans anyway because the association's president was her campaign leader. If she is charged under Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019, would the ruling in People v. Asuncion support her acquittal?

alac.answer: No. Unlike in Asuncion, the element of knowledge is present, so Mayor Ana may be held liable under Sec. 3(j).
alac.legal_basis: The elements of Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019 are: (1) knowingly approving or granting any license, permit, privilege or benefit; (2) in favor of any person not qualified for or not legally entitled to it, or a mere representative or dummy of one who is not so qualified or entitled. Knowledge of the grantee's lack of qualification is essential because it is the basis for concluding that the accused acted with bias or partiality, and possibly corruption. In People v. Asuncion (G.R. Nos. 250366 and 250388-98, April 6, 2022), the mayor was acquitted because the prosecution did not prove he knew the grantees were unqualified; their accreditation by the Sanggunian made any lack of qualification not apparent to anyone.
alac.application: Here the association was not qualified under the ordinance because it was never accredited, and Mayor Ana was told so in writing before she acted. Her knowledge is established, and her reason for proceeding (to favor her campaign leader) shows the bias and partiality that the knowledge element is meant to capture. This is favoritism, not an honest mistake of interpretation, so the good-faith reasoning in Asuncion does not apply.
alac.conclusion: Mayor Ana may be convicted under Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019 because she knowingly granted a benefit to an unqualified grantee.

bar_questions.q: Mayor Carlo's wife heads a federation whose chapters received municipal loans that he approved. The disbursements were made under the previous year's annual appropriation ordinance, which was deemed reenacted because the Sangguniang Bayan failed to pass a new one within 90 days from the start of the fiscal year. The prosecution charges the mayor and the chapter presidents with malversation of public funds in conspiracy, relying solely on the mayor's marriage certificate and his wife's certification that she heads the federation. (a) Was malversation committed? (b) Was conspiracy established?

alac.legal_basis: Malversation under Art. 217 of the RPC requires that the accountable public officer appropriated, took or misappropriated public funds, or consented to or, through abandonment or negligence, permitted another to take them. No contract involving the expenditure of public funds may be entered into without a sufficient appropriation (PD 1445, Sec. 85). Under Sec. 323 of the Local Government Code, if the sanggunian fails to enact the annual appropriations ordinance within 90 days from the beginning of the fiscal year, the preceding year's ordinance is deemed reenacted. In People v. Asuncion (G.R. Nos. 250366 and 250388-98, April 6, 2022), malversation failed because the loans were supported by an appropriation ordinance reenacted under Sec. 323, and conspiracy failed because the only evidence was the mayor's marriage to the federation's president; conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt by overt acts showing a conscious common design, and there is no presumption of bad faith in RA 3019 cases.
alac.application: (a) The loans were disbursed under an appropriation ordinance deemed reenacted by operation of Sec. 323 of the LGC. The mayor therefore did not take, misappropriate, or permit the taking of public funds without authority. (b) The marriage certificate and the wife's certification show only a relationship. They show no overt act by which the mayor and the chapter presidents acted together toward a common unlawful purpose, and conspiracy cannot be presumed from kinship.
alac.conclusion: The mayor and the chapter presidents should be acquitted, because neither misappropriation nor conspiracy was proved.

notes: The Court did not discuss the last sentence of Sec. 323 of the LGC (quoted in its footnote 67), which limits the reenacted appropriations to salaries and wages of existing positions, statutory and contractual obligations, and essential operating expenses; it simply held that the disbursements were supported by the reenacted ordinance. The decision calls the disbursements both "financial assistance" (as in the Informations and the stipulation) and loans. The heading of the Sec. 3(j) charge appears in places as "Sec. (j)" in the decision.
